bib.title: Reinforcement Learning: A Comprehensive Overview (Chapter 4: Model-based RL)

read.skipped: No reference list in the extracted chapter (text ends at book p.119); nothing skipped.

question: How can a learned or known world model be used to make RL more sample efficient, through decision-time planning, background planning, and what should the model be trained to predict?
contributions: Taxonomy of MBRL into decision-time planning (MPC/RHC, MCTS, SMC) and background planning (Dyna, Dreamer), Algorithms 12-17
Survey of world-model training targets (observation, reward, value, policy, latent self-prediction) and how they address objective mismatch (Table 4.2)
Treatment of model error, game-theoretic MBRL, and predictive representations (GVF, successor representations/features/measures)

results.claim: Learning the dynamics model needs fewer samples than learning the policy, which motivates MBRL.
results.setup: Theoretical statement in the chapter introduction; no setting given.
results.quote: It can be shown that the sample complexity of learning the dynamics is less than the sample complexity of learning the policy [ZHR24].1

results.claim: A robot-hand controller needed about 100 years of simulated data to learn Rubik's cube manipulation, cited as model-free sample inefficiency.
results.quote: needs 100 years of simulated data to learn to manipulate a rubiks cube.

results.claim: Forward search to depth d costs exponential time in d; sparse sampling replaces |S| by m sampled next states, making cost independent of |S|.
results.setup: Tree search over a model with |S| states, |A| actions, depth d, m samples per action (O((|S|x|A|)^d) vs O((m x |A|)^d)).

results.claim: Worked example: open-loop planning picks 'down' with expected reward 20, but closed-loop planning can guarantee 30, so open-loop MPC is suboptimal in stochastic environments.
results.setup: Fig 4.3: 9 states, 2 actions, horizon d=2; only up from s1 is stochastic (s2 or s3 with p 0.5). Open-loop plan utilities: (up,up)=15, (up,down)=15, (down,up)=20, (down,down)=20.

results.claim: EfficientZero adds a self-prediction loss, an LSTM value prefix and Reanalyse leaf-value refresh to MuZero; all three help but the self-prediction loss gives the biggest gain.
results.setup: Ablation reported in EfficientZero paper; no numbers given in this chapter.
results.quote: but the biggest gain is from the self-prediction loss.

results.claim: DreamerV3 was the first method to obtain diamonds in Minecraft without human demonstrations, but it took 17 days of training.
results.setup: DreamerV3, Minecraft diamond task, no human demonstration data.
results.quote: (However, reaching this goal took 17 days of training.)

results.claim: DreamerV4's world model is a latent video diffusion transformer trained offline on reward-free action-labelled Minecraft video, then a policy is trained purely in imagination.
results.setup: DreamerV4: conditional latent video diffusion, context length c; policy initialised by behaviour cloning then actor-critic in imagination with Minecraft reward functions learned from VPT metadata.
results.quote: offline on 2500 hours of reward-free but action-labeled videos (keyboard-mouse actions) of people playing

results.claim: DreamerV4 cuts diffusion sampling to 1-2 steps with the shortcut trick, because iterative diffusion makes the world model slow to sample.
results.quote: reduce the number of diffusion sampling steps to 1-2.

results.claim: JEPA-style encoders compress a 224x224x3 image into an embedding of about 1024, an information bottleneck that helps avoid latent collapse.
results.setup: ViT encoder example; input 224 x 224 x 3 = 150,528 values.
results.quote: which often amounts to an embedding size of ∼1024.

results.claim: Successor representation example: under a random policy M(s13,s14)=5.97 and M(s13,s12)=0.16 in a 2D maze.
results.setup: Fig 4.10: 2D maze, reward -0.1 everywhere except goal 1.0; random policy. Under optimal policy the same entries are 1.0 and 0.66.
results.quote: (e.g., M π(s13, s14) = 5.97) and low values to states that are further away (e.g., M π(s13, s12) = 0.16).

limits: Survey: no experiments of its own; every empirical statement is cited from other work and numbers are rare.
Convergence of self-predictive (EMA/stop-gradient) world models is proven only for linear encoders; the general nonlinear case is stated as open (Sec 4.4.2.7).
VICReg/Barlow Twins give an upper, not lower, bound on information I(z), so they do not strictly optimise Eq 4.34 (Sec 4.4.2.8).
CTRL closed-loop transcription is designed for iid images; extension to sequential world models is open (Sec 4.4.2.9).
Self-play AlphaZero-style agents remain open to adversarial attack; [Wan+23] showed humans can beat superhuman Go agents (Sec 4.2.2.1).
Successor representations assume a finite discrete state space and are policy dependent (Sec 4.5.2).
Model-free vs model-based: a limited-capacity model can be dominated by model-free RL (Sec 4.4.4.3).
Some on-policy methods are technically invalid with Dyna unless the replay buffer is not too stale (Sec 4.3.2.2).
practices: Interleave model learning and policy learning rather than learn a model once and plan, because the policy may query states with no data (Sec 4.1).
Use decision-time planning when the reward changes or is intrinsic, since the world model can be trained reward-free; accept it is slower (Sec 4.1).
Amortise planning into a reactive policy via background planning (Dyna, Dreamer) when decision-time search is too slow (Sec 4.3).
Start imagined rollouts from previously visited real states and keep them short (MBPO) to limit compounding model error (Sec 4.4.4.1).
In Dyna with function approximation, train the policy on real plus imagined data, with an off-policy learner for replayed data; gradually raise the real-data fraction per [Lai+21] (Sec 4.3.2.2).
Prefer latent prediction targets (reward, value, policy, self-prediction) over full observation prediction to avoid objective mismatch and distractors (Sec 4.4.2).
Prevent self-prediction collapse with a frozen EMA target network plus stop-gradient, or with variance/covariance regularisers (Sec 4.4.2.7-4.4.2.8).
Use symlog or log-transformed discretised cross-entropy for rewards/values to be robust to scale (DreamerV3, TD-MPC2) (Sec 4.4.1.3, 4.4.2.12).
Fall back to a model-free policy when the model-based policy is not confidently better (Sec 4.4.4.3).
Use successor features plus generalised policy improvement to reuse a policy library on a new reward weight w without relearning (Sec 4.5.3.1).

terms.definition: learn the state transition or dynamics model pS(s'|s,a), also called a world model, and the reward function R(s,a), then use them to compute a policy
use the model to choose the next action by searching over possible future trajectories, score each, pick the best first action, step, and repeat
use the current model and policy to roll out imaginary trajectories and improve the policy with model-free RL on them
plan from the current state to a fixed depth d, take the first action, observe the new state, and replan
sample a subset of m possible next states per action in forward search, complexity O((m x |A|)^d), independent of |S|
MCTS action selection a = argmax Q(s,a) + c sqrt(log N(s)/N(s,a)); with prior P(s,a): Q + c P(s,a) sqrt(N(s))/(1+N(s,a))
choose the sequence of future actions without knowing the future states, then replan each step
sample action sequences from a proposal and keep the best; CEM refits a Gaussian to the top K; MPPI is a CEM variant whose Gaussian mean is the previous reference trajectory shifted one step
train the policy on real data and imaginary model data, while the model is trained in parallel; a hybrid model-free/model-based method
ordered game where policy is leader (PAL) or model is leader (MAL), with provable local convergence, replacing unstable simultaneous gradient descent ascent
the discrepancy between how a model is trained (predict observations) and how its representation is used for control
two states are value equivalent given a policy if V^pi(s1)=V^pi(s2); an optimal representation maps h_i,h_j to the same z only if Q*(h_i,a)=Q*(h_j,a)
states s1,s2 are bisimilar if P(s'|s1,a) ~ P(s'|s2,a) and R(s1,a)=R(s2,a); stronger than value equivalence and policy independent
trivially minimising self-prediction loss by mapping everything to a constant embedding
V^{pi,C,gamma}(s)=E[sum gamma^t C(s_{t+1})], the discounted sum of a cumulant C instead of reward
M^pi(s,s~)=E[sum gamma^t I(s_{t+1}=s~)]; in matrix form T^pi (I - gamma T^pi)^-1; gives V for any reward as sum M(s,s~)R(s~)
SF psi^pi(s)=E[sum gamma^t phi(s_{t+1})]; with R=phi^T w, V=psi^T w; generalised policy improvement a*=argmax_a max_i psi^{pi_i}(s,a)^T w_new
mu^pi(s~|s)=(1-gamma) sum gamma^t P(s_{t+1}=s~|s_0=s), a normalised SR usable with continuous states

code.snippet: MBRL-agent loop: collect tau_env=rollout(s,pi,T,M_env); D=D U tau_env; update model online/by replay; update policy (pi,V) on-policy/off-policy with real/imaginary rollouts, until converged
l(M) = -1/(NT) sum_n sum_{(s_t,a_t,r_{t+1},s_{t+1}) in tau^n} log M(s_{t+1}, r_{t+1} | s_t, a_t)  // NLL;  M = M - eta_M grad_M l(M)
a = argmax_{a in A(s)} Q(s,a) + c sqrt(log N(s) / N(s,a))   (UCT);  prior form Eq 4.2: Q(s,a) + c P(s,a) sqrt(N(s)) / (1 + N(s,a))
L(theta) = E[(V_MCTS(s) - V_theta(s))^2 - sum_a pi_MCTS_s(a) log pi_theta(a|s)];  pi_MCTS_s(a) = [N(s,a)/sum_b N(s,b)]^(1/tau)
SMC planning: q(tau) ∝ d_q(s0) prod_t T(s_{t+1}|s_t,a_t) pi(a_t|s_t) exp(A(s_t,a_t)/eta); particle weight w(tau_1:t) ∝ w(tau_1:t-1) exp(A(s_t,a_t)/eta)
Tabular Dyna-Q: real step then Q(s,a) += eta[r + gamma max_a' Q(s',a') - Q(s,a)]; M_hat(s,a)=(s',r); then N times sample (s,a) from D, (s',r)=M_hat(s,a), same Q update
L_EZP = || M_theta(E_phi(h,a)) - sg(E_phi_bar(h')) ||_2^2 ; phi_bar_t = rho phi_bar + (1-rho) phi_bar_{t-1}  (EMA frozen target)
TD-MPC2 loss: L = E sum_t lambda^t ( ||z'_t - sg(E(o'_t))||^2 + CE(r_hat_t, r_t) + CE(q_hat_t, q_t) )
M^pi = T^pi (I - gamma T^pi)^-1 ;  V^{R,pi}(s) = sum_s~ M^pi(s,s~) R(s~)
a*(s; w_new) = argmax_a max_i psi^{pi_i}(s,a)^T w_new   (GPI)
